 2                    I.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

 3   Q.   ARE YOU THE SAME JARED GURLEY WHO FILED DIRECT

 4        TESTIMONY        ON   BEHALF       OF   ONCOR       ELECTRIC       DELIVERY

 5        COMPANY LLC (“ONCOR”) AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES

 6        CORPORATION (“LCRA TSC”) (“APPLICANTS”) IN THIS DOCKET?

 7   A.   Yes.

 8   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

 9   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to address and respond to issues

10        raised in the direct testimonies of intervenor witnesses challenging the need

11        for, and alternatives to, the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, Permian Basin

12        Import Path 2, the Bell County East – Big Hill 765 kilovolt (“kV”) transmission

13        line project (“Proposed Transmission Line Project”), and the Big Hill – Sand

14        Lake 765 kV transmission line project. My rebuttal testimony addresses

15        these issues from a system-planning perspective. Applicants’ witness Mr.

16        Collin Martin addresses some of the same issues from an transmission

17        operations perspective, based as his experience in various roles with

18        Oncor’s Transmission Grid Operations group.

19   Q.   IF YOU DO NOT ADDRESS A SPECIFIC CLAIM OR INTERVENOR’S

20        TESTIMONY IN YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY, DOES THAT INDICATE

21        THAT YOU AGREE WITH OR CONCEDE THE ISSUES THEY RAISED?

                                                     Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

  1   A.   No. Hundreds of parties filed testimony in this docket, many of which raised

 2        substantially the same issues. Therefore, my rebuttal testimony addresses

 3        the issues raised in intervenor testimony without listing each individual party

 4        who raised them. While I frequently cite specific intervenor testimonies, that

 5        does not indicate that my response only applies to that party’s concern or

 6        or that I am not addressing similar issues voiced by other parties.

 7   Q.   WAS YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER

 8        YOUR DIRECT SUPERVISION AND CONTROL?

 9   A.   Yes.

10          II.    HOUSE BILL 5066 REQUIRES A TRANSMISSION PLAN

11   Q.   INTERVENOR BOBBY DON HART (PAGE 6, LINES 53-59) ARGUES

12        THAT THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE EXCEEDS THE

13        INTENDED SCOPE OF HOUSE BILL (HB) 5066. DO YOU AGREE?

14   A.   No. HB 5066 amended the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) by adding

15        PURA §§ 39.166 and .167, among other things. With regard to the Permian

16        Basin Reliability Plan, PURA § 39.167 stated that:

17                Not later than January 30, 2024, the commission shall
18                direct the independent organization certified under Section
19                39.151 for the ERCOT power region to develop a reliability
20                plan under Section 39.166 for the Permian Basin region ....
21                The plan must: (1) address extending transmission service
22                to areas where mineral resources have been found;
23                (2) address increasing available capacity to meet
24                forecasted load; and (3) provide available infrastructure to
25                reduce interconnection times in areas without access to
26                transmission service.


     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                 Gurley – Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                            -3-
  1          A copy of HB 5066 is attached to my rebuttal testimony as Exhibit JG-R-1.

 2          ERCOT is the independent organization under PURA § 39.151, and in that

 3          role, ERCOT is responsible for: (1) ensuring access to the transmission

 4          system for all buyers and sellers of electricity, and (2) ensuring the reliability

 5          and adequacy of the regional electrical network. In the Permian Basin

 6          Reliability Plan, ERCOT explains how the necessary transmission upgrades

 7          satisfy each requirements of HB 5066. Local transmission upgrades fulfill

 8          the directives to “address extending transmission service to areas where

 9          mineral resources have been found” and “provide available infrastructure to

10          meet forecasted load,” while import paths “address increasing available

11          capacity to meet forecasted load.”

12                 As Oncor witness Mr. Martin explains in his rebuttal testimony, a lack

13          of adequate transmission capacity is currently limiting load-serving

14          capabilities in the Permian Basin, and those limitations will tighten as the

15          forecasted load materializes.        Import Path 2 will increase available

16          transmission capacity to ensure the transmission system has adequate

17          capacity available to reliably serve the forecasted load. Therefore, Import

18          Path 2 is well within the scope of both HB 5066 and ERCOT’s

19          responsibilities under PURA § 39.151.

20        III.   THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IS NEEDED

21   Q.     A NUMBER OF INTERVENORS CHALLENGE THE NEED FOR THE

22          PROJECT. FOR EXAMPLE, COMMISSIONER DAMON BEIERLE OF

     PUC Docket No. 59475                                   Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                        Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

  1        SAN SABA COUNTY CLAIMS THERE IS A LACK OF TRANSPARENCY

 2        AND CLEAR, INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS

 3        NECESSARY. HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

 4   A.   I disagree. The evidence is well-established and widely available. As I

 5        explained above, ERCOT is the independent organization charged with

 6        planning an adequate and reliable transmission system. ERCOT studied

 7        the transmission needs of the Permian Basin region over the course of

 8        seven months to identify the necessary transmission improvements for the

 9        Permian Basin Reliability Plan. Then ERCOT studied alternative, statewide

10        reliability plans at different voltage classes before the Commission selected

11        the 765 kV alternative, including Import Path 2.         This process was

12        conducted in full view of the public and with substantial input and feedback

13        from Transmission Service Providers (“TSPs”), Commission Staff, and

14        other interested stakeholders.    There were multiple public workshops,

15        public deliberations, and opportunities for public comment. The Permian

16        Basin Reliability Plan has been publicly available since July 2024.

17   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE PROCESS ERCOT USED TO IDENTIFY THE

18        NECESSARY TRANSMISSION IMPROVEMENTS IN THE PERMIAN

19        BASIN RELIABILITY PLAN.

20   A.   To identify the necessary upgrades for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan,

21        ERCOT performed reliability assessments based on North American

22        Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1,

 2        studies observed thermal and voltage criteria violations, voltage instability,

 3        and unsolved power flows in the 2030 and 2038 base cases under N-0

 4        (system intact) conditions, demonstrating the need for substantially more

 5        transmission capacity, including multiple import paths, to serve the

 6        forecasted demand. As ERCOT explained in Section 4 of the Permian

 7        Basin Reliability Plan, the import paths are essential because without them

 8        the demand in the Permian Basin cannot be fully served.

10        system performance under pre- and post-contingency conditions and

11        identify the optimal transmission improvements to serve the forecasted

12        load.    Ultimately, ERCOT recommended the projects described in the

13        Permian Basin Reliability Plan, including three alternative import path

14        options at different voltage levels.

15                Before the Commission selected the voltage for the import paths,

16        ERCOT performed additional economic and reliability studies of the 345 kV

17        and 765 kV alternatives in conjunction with the 2024 Regional Transmission

18        Plan (“RTP”). ERCOT published the results of these studies in the 2024

19        Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) 345-kV Plan and Texas 765-kV

20        Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan Comparison, which was attached

21        as Exhibit JG-1 to my direct testimony.           The 765 kV alternative

22        outperformed the 345 kV option on steady state transfer capability, dynamic

 3        ERCOT to “strongly recommend” the 765 kV alternative, which the

 4        Commission selected at the April 24, 2025 open meeting.

 5             Finally, I want to emphasize that existing system conditions validate

 6        the need for Import Path 2. As Applicants’ witness Mr. Martin describes in

 7        detail, the lack of adequate transmission capacity that gave rise to the

 8        Permian Basin Reliability Plan is now causing significant transmission

 9        constraints that put the reliability of the grid at risk across large areas of the

10        state. These are not hypothetical or distant issues. They are persistent

11        operating limits that exist today. Import Path 2 is necessary to resolve those

12        constraints.

13   Q.   DO THE INTERVENORS WHO CHALLENGE THE NEED FOR THE

14        PROJECT OFFER ANY EVIDENCE TO REFUTE ERCOT’S STUDY

15        RESULTS, METHODOLOGY, OR EXISTING SYSTEM LIMITATIONS?

16   A.   No. Instead, they primarily criticize the process, speculate that the demand

17        forecasts underlying the Permian Basin Reliability Plan are overstated, or

18        argue that various alternatives could meet the needs of the Permian Basin,

19        such as new dispatchable or distributed generation, underground lines,

20        microgrids, and others. As I describe in more detail below, these are not

21        viable alternatives. No intervenors have provided a substantive explanation

22        for their belief that ERCOT’s study results are invalid or produced a study

  1        demonstrating that their suggested alternatives could actually eliminate the

 2        need for Import Path 2.

 3   Q.   HOW DO YOU RESPOND TO THE PARTIES WHO CLAIM THE

 4        PERMIAN BASIN LOAD FORECASTS ARE OVERSTATED?

 5   A.   I disagree. ERCOT’s load-forecasting methodology is rooted in the explicit

 6        requirements of HB 5066, which requires the Commission to consider loads

 7        that do not yet have a signed interconnection agreement in evaluating the

 8        need for a new transmission project.      This was an important change

 9        because it will allow transmission development to keep pace with load

10        growth on the planning horizon. Over The last decade, load growth in the

11        Permian Basin has averaged 11% per year. That is not a forecast; it is real,

12        observed, historical demand.

13             As I discussed in my direct testimony, prior to HB 5066, ERCOT and

14        TSPs could not begin developing necessary transmission improvements to

15        serve new customer load until an interconnection agreement was executed,

16        which often does not happen until the customer is far along in its

17        development process. This is one of the main reasons the transmission

18        system has historically failed to keep pace with Permian Basin load growth.

19        The changes resulting from HB 5066 help to align the planning timelines for

20        new transmission infrastructure and the customer loads it will serve.

21             Furthermore, the forecasts used for the 2024 RTP, where ERCOT

22        studied the alternative voltage classes for the import paths, were

     PUC Docket No. 59475                              Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                   Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                          -8-
  1        deliberately reduced from the forecasts submitted by TSPs, which

 2        themselves included only the loads the TSPs deemed likely to materialize.

 3        The forecasts ERCOT used only include 27.6% of the TSPs’ forecasted

 4        load. The Commission factored these reductions into its evaluation of the

 5        alternative voltage class options, which ultimately resulted in its approval of

 6        the 765 kV import paths. The 2024 RTP is included as Exhibit JG-R-2 to

 7        my rebuttal testimony. Intervenor Tom Green filed third-party testimony

 8        claiming that advances in computing technology will soon make centralized,

 9        large-scale data centers, and thus load forecasts that include them,

10        obsolete. I claim no expertise in computing architecture or data center

11        development.     I can say, though, that future advances in computing

12        architecture do not seemed to have dampened the anticipated electric

13        demand of data center developers across the ERCOT power region.

14             Finally, while the recent growth in electric demand is historically

15        unprecedented, it is not unique to ERCOT. As I explained in my direct

16        testimony, other Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTOs”) across the

17        country are facing similar growth, and many of them are also concluding

18        that 765 kV infrastructure is necessary to meet the demand. For example,

19        the Southwest Power Pool recently approved its first 765 kV transmission

20        line to improve transmission service to historically underserved areas in

21        portions of the Permian Basin located in southeastern New Mexico. Given

22        that the same trend is occurring directly next door to ERCOT, in a

 2        it would be imprudent to not build the transmission capacity needed to serve

 3        the forecasted load based only on a hunch that the demand won’t actually

 4        materialize. This is especially true in light of the measures the Commission,

 5        ERCOT, and TSPs have taken to ensure that only loads that are likely to

 6        materialize are included in the demand forecasts.

  1             Moreover, as Mr. Martin explains in his rebuttal testimony, all three of

 6   Q.   SOME INTERVENORS, SUCH AS TIMOTHY HEFNER, ON BEHALF OF

 7        COMANCHE CREEK PARTNERS (PAGE 17, LINES 15-17)                         AND

 8        CLAUDIA CABANISS (PAGE 7) SUGGEST THAT THIS LINE WILL

 9        SERVE PRIVATE OIL AND GAS OR DATA CENTER CUSTOMERS AND

10        NOT THE PUBLIC. IS THIS ACCURATE?

11        No. This project, like most networked transmission lines, will not provide

12        service directly to any single end-use customer or class of customers. New

13        transmission infrastructure is commonly built or expanded to improve

14        transmission service in specific areas that are experiencing rapid economic

15        or population growth.    For example, between 2022 and 2024, Oncor

16        obtained approvals for the Roanoke Area Upgrades Project, which

17        consisted of a series of transmission upgrades to improve reliability and

18        load-serving capabilities in Wise, Denton, and Tarrant counties. Similar to

19        the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, the Roanoke Area Upgrades Project was

20        needed to address local load growth, which in that case was driven by

21        population growth and rapid suburban development.

22             The purpose of the high-voltage transmission system is to efficiently

     PUC Docket No. 59475                               Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                    Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

  1        transfer bulk power where it is needed so it can be delivered to all end-use

 2        customers. Most of those customers are private entities, whether they are

 3        households, small businesses, or large commercial and industrial

 4        consumers.     Applicants have a duty to provide all customers with

 5        continuous, adequate and reliable transmission service. The fact that the

 6        transmission system is built and expanded to reliably serve all customers

 7        within ERCOT’s footprint is exactly what makes transmission improvements

 8        like this one a public use and benefit.

 9   Q.   SOME INTERVENORS, INCLUDING DAVID NICHOLLS (PDF PAGE 8),

10        ASSERT       THAT    THE    PROJECT       WILL     NOT    BENEFIT      THEIR

11        COMMUNITIES BECAUSE IT TERMINATES IN THE PERMIAN BASIN.

12        HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

13   A.   These assertions misunderstand how customers will benefit from the

14        Project. It’s true that Import Path 2 traverses communities with no station

15        endpoint. But all three of the stations along Import Path 2 will connect

16        directly to the 345 kV transmission system, which serves the entire state,

17        including the Permian Basin. As discussed in my direct testimony, this

18        Project, in conjunction with the other Permian Basin Reliability Plan

19        transmission upgrades, will improve the reliability, strength, and stability of

20        the overall transmission system, and those benefits will flow to all ERCOT

21        customers.

22             More specifically, the 765 kV import paths will improve bi-directional

     PUC Docket No. 59475                                Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                           - 13 -
  1        power flows between West Texas and load centers, which will help to

 2        alleviate costly transmission congestion and reduce the need to curtail

 3        Permian Basin exports of cost-effective renewable generation. The 765 kV

 4        network will also improve operational flexibility, allowing for more cost-

 5        effective operations and maintenance on the lower-voltage systems that

 6        serve all end-use customers. Additionally, 765 kV facilities will experience

 7        fewer line losses and make more efficient use of right-of-way, which will

 8        ultimately benefit landowners by reducing the amount of new right-of-way

 9        required compared with a 345 kV solution. ERCOT confirmed each of these

10        benefits in its 765/345 kV comparison report.

11             While the Applicants do not provide retail delivery service to every

12        end-use customer in the study area, all ERCOT utilities—and ultimately, all

13        retail customers—take service from the same transmission system. That

14        system is an integrated and interconnected network, so conditions in one

15        area can impact reliability and system stability over a much broader area.

16   Q.   MANY INTERVENOR TESTIMONIES QUESTION WHETHER THE

17        PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT WILL LOWER THEIR

18        COSTS. HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

19   A.   Based on my review of intervenor testimonies, it appears that many

20        intervenors raise this issue with regard to PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E), which

21        requires the Commission to consider “the probable improvement of service

22        or lowering of cost to consumers in the area if the certificate is granted[.]”

     PUC Docket No. 59475                               Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                    Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                          - 14 -
  1        My understanding of this provision is that the “probable improvement of

 2        service” consideration generally applies to reliability projects while “lowering

 3        of cost to consumers” generally applies to economic projects. Import Path 2

 4        is a reliability project that will improve service to consumers.

 5              There are significant avoided costs, cost savings, and other benefits

 6        associated with the Proposed Transmission Line Project and the 765 kV

 7        transmission facilities more broadly when compared to a 345 kV alternative.

 8        ERCOT laid out some of these benefits in the 765/345 kV comparison

 9        included as Exhibit 4 to my direct testimony. They include $890 million less

10        in construction-related outage costs, $229 million more annual consumer

11        energy cost savings, $28 million more annual production cost savings, 5%

12        (560 GWh) less energy loss each year, 1,443 fewer miles of existing facility

13        upgrades, and up to 3 GW of additional transfer capacity. These benefits

14        must be considered alongside the comparable costs for construction and

15        maintenance of the 765 kV and 345 kV alternatives.

16              It is also important to remember that the Commission is in the process

17        of revising its transmission cost allocation, as required by Senate Bill 6.

18        Since this revision is still in progress, it has not been factored into the

19        estimated customer bill impacts offered by certain intervenors.

20        IV.      IMPORT PATH 2 IS SUPERIOR TO OTHER ALTERNATIVES
21   Q.   SEVERAL INTERVENORS, INCLUDING JUDI GRACY (PAGES 5-6 &

22        EXHIBIT A), MARK FRIESENHAHN (PAGES 5-10), AND MICHAEL


     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                 Gurley – Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                     Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                           - 15 -
  1        MCWILLIAMS (PAGE 15, LINE 25 TO PAGE 16, LINE 2), ARGUE FOR

 2        GENERATION ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION

 3        LINE PROJECT. IS GENERATION A VIABLE ALTERNATIVE?

 4   A.   No.    New generation is not a viable alternative to the Proposed

 5        Transmission Line Project for several reasons.                First, HB 5066

 6        contemplated a transmission reliability plan and made ERCOT, the entity

 7        that oversees transmission planning and reliability, responsible for

 8        developing that plan.         Generation alone cannot extend transmission

 9        service, cannot make additional capacity available to serve load, and cannot

10        reduce transmission interconnection times. These are the objectives of

11        HB 5066, and they are transmission objectives.

12              Second,    under       the   existing   market   framework,   neither   the

13        Commission nor ERCOT can simply order generation to be built, and Oncor

14        cannot build or own generation. Electricity generation is deregulated in the

15        ERCOT market, which means that private entities determine when and

16        where new generation resources will be built. If any region within ERCOT

17        lacks sufficient generation capacity to serve its own demand, new

18        transmission is the primary tool at the Commission’s and ERCOT’s disposal

19        to address that shortfall.

20              Third, any benefit of additional generation capacity is limited by

21        existing constraints on the 345 kV transmission network. ERCOT routinely

22        denies requests to take even a single line out of service for scheduled

     SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                                     Gurley – Rebuttal
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                    Oncor Electric & LCRA TSC
                                                         Bell County East – Big Hill CCN

                                              - 16 -
  1        maintenance or construction because the system does not have enough

 2        transfer capacity to bear the loss without a significant risk of overloading.

 3        Those areas include ERCOT’s West/Far West weather zones, which cover

 4        the area between North-Central Texas and the Permian Basin. Despite

 5        numerous initiatives to build new 345 kV infrastructure and upgrade aging

 6        facilities over the last decade, demand in the Permian Basin continues to

 7        outpace transfer capacity.    One reason that 765 kV import paths, in

 8        particular, are needed is because they provide six times the capacity of a

 9        single 345 kV circuit and can be built in about the same amount of time.

10        Adding generation capacity without new transmission capacity could

11        exacerbate some of the very same problems the Permian Basin Reliability

12        Plan was intended to solve.

13             Finally, in the time since the Commission approved the 765 kV import

14        paths, ERCOT’s system models have assumed that Import Path 2 and other

15        import path projects will be in service when they are needed.           Any

16        transmission improvements planned since that time were planned for a

17        system that includes Import Path 2 as a primary transfer corridor. Without

18        it, much of the transmission planning that has occurred over the last year

19        would be unwound, placing even more strain on a system that is struggling

20        to meet rising demand.

21   Q.   WERE      NEW     GENERATION             RESOURCES     CONSIDERED         IN

22        CONNECTION WITH THE PERMIAN BASIN RELIABILITY PLAN?

                                          - 17 -
  1   A.   Yes. In studying the reliability needs of the Permian Basin, ERCOT added

 2        over 17,000 MW of planned generation capacity to its models, which

 3        allowed it to identify the specific upgrades needed to provide reliable

 4        transmission service. Then, in the 2024 RTP, ERCOT identified a system-

 5        wide generation deficit of more than 11 gigawatts (“GW”), even after adding

 6        all planned generation resources in the interconnection queue to the study

 7        case. This underscores the need for additional transmission capacity to

 8        efficiently and cost-effectively transfer existing and planned generation

 9        capacity to the locations where it is needed.

10              Moreover, in the same year that HB 5066 became law, the Texas

11        Legislature also established the Texas Energy Fund (“TEF”) to incentivize

12        the construction of new dispatchable generation with low-interest loans and

13        completion bonus grants. Because the generation market in ERCOT is

14        competitive, these types of market-based incentives can be useful tools to

15        encourage the construction of new generation. However, the decision of

16        where and when to propose new resources still rests with private companies

17        who are largely motivated by their own economic interests, so those tools

18        lack the precision of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, which provides

19        transmission solutions tailored to the needs of the system as a whole. This

20        is evidenced by the fact that only 2.5 GW of TEF generation is currently

21        planned for the Permian Basin.

22   Q.   ARE    THERE     OTHER      REASONS       TO    BELIEVE   THAT     LOCAL

Executive Summary
The 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) is the result of a coordinated planning process performed
by ERCOT Grid Planning with extensive review and input by Transmission Planners (TPs) and
Transmission Owners (TOs) registered with North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC),
and other stakeholders. The 2024 RTP addresses ERCOT System transmission needs for years 2026
through 2030. This report documents the results of the assessment, in part, to comply with the
requirements of NERC Reliability Standards, ERCOT Protocols, and the ERCOT Planning Guide.

The reliability analysis was performed over a 6-year planning horizon; years 2 through 5 representing
the near-term horizon, and year 6 representing the long-term horizon. The 2024 RTP assessed
ERCOT’s steady-state transmission needs under summer peak and off-peak conditions. In addition to
the seasonal variations, the 2024 RTP also included sensitivity analyses to address uncertainty
involved in the transmission planning process. The reliability analysis in the 2024 RTP included:

    •   Steady-state contingency analysis to identify criteria violations based on NERC Reliability
        Standards and ERCOT planning criteria;

    •   Short-circuit analysis to identify over-dutied circuit breakers in the near-term planning horizon;
        and

    •   Cascading analysis to identify potential system cascading conditions.

Following the reliability assessment, ERCOT, in collaboration with TPs, developed Corrective Action
Plans (CAPs) to address the reliability criteria violations identified in this assessment. These plans
included, but were not limited to, upgrades or additions of new transmission facilities and new
Constraint Management Plans (CMPs).

The ERCOT System is experiencing rapid changes, including trends of notable growth in demand and
penetration of intermittent Generation Resources. On August 10, 2023, ERCOT set the current all-
time peak demand record of 85,508 MW, surpassing the previous record of 80,148 MW set in 2022.
This trend of rising demand is expected to continue, driven by factors such as the further electrification
of oil and gas processes in the Permian Basin and continued interest in connecting large loads to the
ERCOT System. Sufficient transmission capacity plays a key role in ensuring system reliability while
meeting the rapid growth in demand. While transmission still typically requires 3 to 5 years to be
developed and energized, demand growth is escalating as new large loads are added to the ERCOT
System faster (6 to 12 months) and in greater sizes than historical load interconnections.

As the new load interconnection timeline outpaces the development of transmission projects, the
Texas Legislature recognized the need to update rules in the ERCOT Region. Previously, these rules
did not allow ERCOT to include loads in planning studies unless they had executed an interconnection
agreement. Updating these rules is essential to expedite the process in order to reliably serve the
anticipated rapid demand growth. In December 2022, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT)
amended 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101 to implement Senate Bill (SB) 1281 (87th

These new requirements combined with unprecedented economic growth led to a significant increase

exceeded 150 GW, of which approximately 50 GW is large load. Close to 40 GW of that forecasted

While the new rules allow for the consideration of more load in the planning processes, the policy
governing the inclusion of planned Generation Resources in the planning models remains unchanged.
Currently, planned Generation Resources can only be added to the planning models when they meet
the requirements established in paragraph (1) of the ERCOT Planning Guide Section 6.9, Addition of
Proposed Generation to the Planning Models. Under this rule, the total available generation was less
than 120 GW in the 2030 summer peak case, based on the 2024 RTP renewable and battery dispatch
assumptions. This indicated a supply deficit of more than 30 GW to meet the demand. Additional steps
outside of the current planning practices were needed to create planning models capable of
accommodating the unprecedented load growth. To achieve a balance between supply and demand,
ERCOT incorporated generators that have not yet met the Planning Guide Section 6.9 requirements
into the planning models and presented the assumptions1 at the May 2024 Regional Planning Group
(RPG) meeting. ERCOT is currently developing a Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) to adjust
the criteria for adding Generation Resources to the planning models and will initiate stakeholder
discussions on this topic in 2025.

In addition to the magnitude of the load growth, the “flat” or constant nature of the large loads adds
another layer of complexity. Most of the large loads seeking interconnection are expected to maintain
consistent electricity consumption regardless of season, day, or time. Ensuring reliable interconnection
for these loads requires a resource mix capable of supporting their 24/7 demand. According to the
capacity expansion results from the 2024 ERCOT Long-Term System Assessment (LTSA) high large
load adoption scenario, this resource mix requires additional dispatchable Generation Resources.

The new load forecast in the ERCOT Region creates significant investment opportunities for balanced
generation growth. The right resource mix needs to be carefully considered to address not only the
magnitude of the load growth but also its unique characteristics.

4.1.      Study Assumptions and Methodology

Pursuant to the amended 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i), an economic cost-benefit study for economic
projects must be performed under a CCS test and a PCS test. Until the CCS test becomes effective,
§ 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i)(I)(-b-) allows ERCOT to use the GRR test, which was used for evaluation of
economically driven projects in the ERCOT Region during the 2006 to 2012 timeframe as the
congestion cost savings test. To pass the PCS test, the levelized ERCOT-wide annual PCS
attributable to the proposed project should be equal to or greater than the first-year annual revenue
requirement (12.9%) of the proposed project. To satisfy the GRR test requirement, the levelized
ERCOT-wide annual GRR attributable to the proposed project should be equal to or greater than the
average of the annual revenue requirement for the first three years (12.6%) of the proposed project.
These revenue requirements are reviewed annually and may vary from year to year. ERCOT may

Executive Summary
The 2025 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) is the result of a coordinated planning process performed
by ERCOT Grid Planning with extensive review and input by Transmission Planners (TPs) and
Transmission Owners (TOs) registered with North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC),
and other stakeholders. The 2025 RTP addresses ERCOT System transmission needs for years 2027
through 2031, based on the assessment of various factors, including reliability and economic analyses.
This report documents the results of the assessment, in part, to comply with the requirements of NERC
Reliability Standards, ERCOT Protocols, and the ERCOT Planning Guide.

The reliability analysis was performed over a six-year planning horizon; years two through five
representing the near-term horizon and year six representing the long-term horizon. The 2025 RTP
assessed ERCOT’s steady-state transmission needs under summer peak and off-peak conditions. In
addition to the seasonal variations, the 2025 RTP also included sensitivity analyses to address
uncertainty involved in the transmission planning process. The reliability analysis in the 2025 RTP
included:

    •   Steady-state contingency analysis to identify criteria violations based on NERC Reliability
        Standards and ERCOT planning criteria

    •   Short circuit analysis to identify over-dutied circuit breakers in the near-term planning horizon

    •   Cascading analysis to identify potential system cascading conditions

Following the reliability analysis, ERCOT, in collaboration with TPs, developed Corrective Action Plans
(CAPs) to address the reliability criteria violations identified. These plans included, but were not limited
to, upgrades or the addition of new transmission facilities and new Constraint Management Plans
(CMPs).

The ERCOT System is experiencing rapid changes, including trends of notable growth in demand and
penetration of intermittent Generation Resources. This trend of rising demand is expected to continue,
driven by factors such as the further electrification of oil and gas processes in the Permian Basin and
continued interest in connecting large loads to the ERCOT System. Sufficient transmission capacity
plays a key role in ensuring system reliability while meeting the rapid demand growth. While
transmission still requires three to five years to be energized, demand is escalating as new large loads
are added to the ERCOT System faster (six to 12 months) and in greater sizes than historical
interconnections.

As the new load interconnection timeline outpaces the development of transmission projects, the
Texas Legislature recognized the need to update rules in the ERCOT Region. Previously, these rules
did not allow ERCOT to include loads in planning studies without signed interconnection agreements.
In December 2022, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) amended 16 Texas Administrative
Code (TAC) § 25.101, Certification Criteria, to implement Senate Bill 1281 (87th Legislative Session).
The amendment included the requirement for any review conducted by ERCOT to incorporate

historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection. In June
2023, House Bill (HB) 5066 (88th Legislative Session) was enacted, introducing a new requirement to
consider loads for which the electric utility has yet to sign an interconnection agreement, as determined
by the electric utility responsible for serving the load.

These new requirements were first implemented in the 2024 RTP and led to a significant increase in
large loads included in that assessment (i.e., data centers, crypto mining, hydrogen and hydrogen-
related manufacturing, and electrification). In the 2024 RTP, the forecasted summer peak demand for
2030 exceeded 150 gigawatts (GW), with close to 40 GW attributed to large loads seeking
interconnections under the new requirements.

The large loads submitted by Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) for consideration under these
requirements in the 2025 RTP were significantly greater compared to the 2024 RTP. The forecasted
summer peak demand for 2031 would have exceeded 218 GW if all TSP-submitted large loads were
included. After performing a historical analysis on large load realization, ERCOT developed an ERCOT
Transmission Planning Adjusted Load Forecast (ETPALF), which adjusted the 2031 forecast from 218
GW to 159 GW. The ETPALF preserved large loads substantiated with an interconnection agreement
at 100%; large loads substantiated with officer attestations (“Officer Letters”) were reduced to 55.4%;
and, data center officer letter loads (OLLs) were further reduced to 49.8% of the initial OLL reduction,
resulting in a final amount that was 27.6% of the full data center value.

On May 1, 2025, ERCOT filed a Good Cause Exception (GCE)1 to the PUCT requesting use of the
ETPALF in the 2025 RTP. The PUCT approved the GCE on June 5, 2025. ERCOT received final load
substantiations from certificated Load Serving Entities at the end of June, and it was not until August
5, 2025, that the start cases for the 2025 RTP were finalized and posted. The delay in the finalization
and posting of the start cases resulted in insufficient time for ERCOT to complete all required
components of the 2025 RTP by the end of the 2025 as required by ERCOT Planning Guide Section
3.1.1.2(2). Accordingly, on November 12, 2025, ERCOT filed a second GCE2 requesting approval to
not perform the Maintenance Outage analysis3 for 2025 RTP as required by ERCOT Planning Guide
Section 4.1.1.8. The PUCT approved the GCE request on December 12, 2025.

While the new requirements identified above allow for the consideration of more load in the planning
processes, the policy governing the inclusion of planned Generation Resources in the planning models
remains unchanged. Currently, planned Generation Resources can only be added to the planning
models when they meet the requirements established under ERCOT Planning Guide Section 6.9,
Addition of Proposed Generation to the Planning Models. Under Planning Guide Section 6.9 criteria,
the total available generation was approximately 130 GW in the 2031 summer peak case based on
the 2025 RTP renewable and battery dispatch assumptions. This indicated a supply deficit of
approximately 30 GW to meet the demand. Additional steps outside of the current planning practices

The recent unprecedented load growth first sparked discussions in the 2024 RTP about introducing
an Extra High Voltage (EHV) 765-kilovolt (kV) backbone infrastructure to the ERCOT Region. This
EHV backbone would function as a superhighway, enabling electrons to flow more efficiently through
long-distance transmission from resource-rich regions to load centers. The benefits of higher voltage
transmission include:

    •   Increased transfer capability to load centers

    •   Flexibility in Generation Resource siting

    •   Increased outage coordination capacity

    •   Reduced impact to Texas consumers due to less overall Right-of-Way requirements5

    •   Reduced line losses

    •   Potential retirement of series compensation devices

    •   Potential exit strategy for some current Generic Transmission Constraints

In July 2024, ERCOT filed the Permian Basin Reliability Plan6 with the PUCT, which identified various
345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import path options to address the reliability needs in the Permian Basin
area. The PUCT approved the Permian Basin Reliability Plan in October 2024, and on May 1, 2025,
approved the 765-kV import option, introducing a higher transmission voltage level in ERCOT for the
first time since the 1960s. In December 2025, ERCOT’s Board of Directors approved the 765-kV
Eastern Backbone and Western Loop projects, thereby approving the full 765-kV Strategic
Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP)7.

The 765-kV STEP was included in the 2025 RTP and showed continued reliability benefits seen in the
2024 RTP. The 2025 RTP evaluated the potential addition of 765-kV equipment beyond what is
already included in the STEP to address new load growth, and additional 765-kV equipment was
ultimately added to address a growing import need in Central Texas.

Unprecedented load growth, insufficient generation to meet this demand, and the faster pace of load
interconnections compared to transmission and generation development moved the ERCOT Region
into a new era of planning. These challenges are further compounded by ongoing changes in the
resource mix. The locations of both load and generation are crucial in driving flow patterns and
determining transmission needs. While the generation interconnection queue offers some insight into
future generation development, the location of future loads is less predictable, especially given the
much shorter lead times for load interconnections. This adds complexity to transmission planning, as
flow patterns and stressed import paths may change between planning cycles. Planning practices and
policies must continue to be reviewed to address these new challenges. ERCOT will continue to work
with stakeholders to identify the necessary changes in the planning processes to ensure system
reliability.

In addition, the rapid growth of wind, solar, and energy storage resources, coupled with increased
retirements of coal and gas generators, led to greater reliance on intermittent, renewable generation
to meet the higher system demand. This resulted in more long-distance power transfers as renewable
generation is typically located far from load centers. Similar to the 2023 and 2024 RTPs, the 2025 RTP
assessment results highlighted the ongoing need for major import pathway enhancements to the
Central Texas corridor. However, with the continued addition of significant amounts of large load in
and around the Corpus Christi area in the 2025 RTP (as first seen in the 2024 RTP), imports to the
Central Texas area primarily come from the Coast Weather Zone, specifically Southwest of Houston,
instead of from South Texas as indicated in the 2023 RTP assessment results.

Overall, 192 reliability projects were identified to address all reliability violations in the 2025 RTP which
included the 765-kV STEP in its base case, compared to 145 projects in the 2024 RTP with the 765-
kV STEP in its base case, and 173 projects in the 2023 RTP. All RTPs from 2023 and earlier did not
include 765-kV STEP in their base cases. This trend emphasizes the transmission challenges
associated with the rapidly changing grid.

2.4.    Reliability Analysis

The reliability analysis in the 2025 RTP was focused on the steady-state analysis requirements of
NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 and the ERCOT Planning Guide. The purpose of the reliability
analysis was to identify potential criteria violations and CAPs that may be used to resolve them. The
RTP analysis included Security Constrained Optimal Power Flow (SCOPF) to identify unresolvable
constraints. Loading and voltage levels of Bulk Electric System (BES) elements were monitored for all

requirements.

The 2025 RTP reliability analysis included the following studies:

   •   SCOPF: Security Constrained Optimal Power Flow (SCOPF) was used to perform basic power
       flow and contingency analysis for P0, P1, P2-1, and P7 planning events. SCOPF used
       generation cost data and other system constraints to give an optimal generation dispatch and
       unit commitment while maintaining the reliability of the system. In this analysis, the software
       simulated the removal of all elements of the Protection System and other automatic controls
       following the contingency event.

       used to test P2-2, P2-3, P2-4, P4, and P5 planning events and extreme events.

Under the ERCOT Planning Guide, reliability projects are those system improvements that are needed
to meet NERC Reliability Standards or ERCOT planning criteria, which could not otherwise be met by
simultaneously feasible, security-constrained re-dispatch of existing and planned generation. To
develop this list of reliability projects, grid simulation software was utilized, which included the removal
of all Protection System elements and other automatic controls following the simulated contingency
events. These elements included devices designed to provide steady-state control of electrical system
quantities, such as on-load tap-changing transformers, phase-shifting transformers, and switched
capacitors and reactors.

A list of potential CAPs, or reliability projects, along with the corresponding limiting elements and
contingencies, was communicated to the appropriate TP and/or TO. TPs and TOs reviewed the initial
list of reliability-driven projects for their technical feasibility and estimated year of completion
(considering necessary lead times). In some cases, the TOs also provided project alternatives. In
instances where it is not feasible to construct a project prior to the identified date of need, ERCOT
designed Constraint Management Plans (CMPs) to mitigate the criteria violations until the permanent
CAP can be put in-service. These mitigation actions were developed in collaboration with TPs and
further communicated to ERCOT Operations. The results were posted on the ERCOT MIS Secure
Area. Study findings were presented to stakeholders at regularly scheduled RPG meetings to solicit

4.6.    Project Evaluation Results

Using the 2025 RTP sensitivity cases for both 2027 and 2030 study years, ERCOT performed an
economic analysis for 12 transmission enhancements chosen based on a review of the initial
congestion patterns and historical data.

Both the congestion cost savings test, measured by the system-wide consumer energy cost reduction,
and the production cost savings test were performed in the project evaluation. The total production
cost is the sum of the fixed operation and maintenance (O&M), startup, variable O&M, fuel, and
emission cost of generators. The total consumer energy cost equals the sum of load payments for
energy use. To pass the production cost savings test, the levelized ERCOT-wide annual production
cost savings attributable to the proposed project should be equal to or greater than the first-year annual
revenue requirement (13.0%) of the proposed project. To satisfy the congestion cost savings test
requirement, the levelized ERCOT-wide annual consumer energy cost reduction attributable to the
proposed project should be equal to or greater than the average of the annual revenue requirement
for the first three years (12.7%) of the proposed project. These revenue requirements are reviewed

3.3.              Peak Net Load ("Sunset") Analysis and Minimum Deliverability

To meet the Minimum Deliverability criteria as required by Planning Guide 4.1.1.7, the 2025 RTP
developed a 2027 study case to represent "sunset" conditions typically found during the 7-8 p.m. time
period.
The battery dispatch of 56.9% was based on the capacity factor observed on October 10,2025, hour
ending (HE) 19 when ERCOT set a battery discharge record of 8,714 MW.

The study condition was further stressed by mimicking a high Southern wind export condition. The
wind and solar capacity factors used in the Sunset BASE case were from August 11,2023, HE20,
when real-time system conditions saw a 345-kV South Texas export line reach 123.2% under a
potential contingency loss. These stressful system conditions were similarto September 6,2023, when
ERCOT entered Energy Emergency Alert conditions. The purpose of this analysis was not to focus
solely on the South Texas export challenge because the future planning project to resolve that issue
has already been ERCOT RPG-approved and will be energized at the point in time at which this study
evaluates. Instead, this analysis was meant to capture what are still the most challenging operating
conditions when solar is very low, wind in the West and Far West is low, and wind in the Panhandle is
very low. These conditions resulted in generation from the Southern and Coast Weather Zones
needing to travel across the entire system, including to the West and Far West Weather Zones,
stressing many paths along the way.
The generation in this case includes only future generation that meets Planning Guide requirements
6.9(1). The load in this study case is approximately 106 GW and contains only large loads with signed
interconnection agreements. This case does not include Officer Letter loads. The system load level is

4.4.1   Top Constraints for Sensitivity Cases

The 2025 RTP economic analysis used the 2027 and 2030 sensitivity cases to assess the cost-
effectiveness of potential transmission improvements for top constraints. Brief descriptions of the top
congestion seen in these cases are presented below, and more details can be found in Appendix P.

In the West and Far West Weather Zones, the rapid growth in renewable generation is expected to
continue. Like the 2024 RTP economic analysis, the WTX interface was the most congested element
observed for both the 2027 and 2030 study years. The interface was congested approximately 24.1%
and 15.8% of hours in the 2027 and 2030 study years, respectively. The congestion rent on this
interface was $245 million in 2027. With the 765-kV STEP incorporated in the 2030 study case, the
congestion rent for the WTX interface remained high at $209 million. Opportunities for further
transmission investment to increase the interface limit should be monitored in the future as renewable
generation buildout continues in the West, Far West, and Panhandle regions.

The North to Houston interface26 showed a congestion rent of $48 million in 2027 and $141 million in
2030. The interface was congested 11.8% of hours in 2027 and 25.6% of hours in 2030 due to rising
energy demand in the greater Houston area.

The Panhandle area is also seeing continuous development of new renewable resources, resulting in
$12 million and $45 million congestion rent in 2027 and 2030, respectively, on the Panhandle interface.
Moreover, in the same area, the Wett Long Draw to Holly POI to Farmland 345-kV line was also among
the top constraints.
The Houdini to WA Parish 345-kV line was projected to incur high congestion rent in 2027 ($150
million). The congestion rent dropped to $22 million in 2030 with the 765-kV STEP incorporated. The
percentage of congestion time dropped from 24.3% of hours in 2027 to 6.7% of hours in 2030.
